cityEvents.title: Alaric's ransom: statues melted, including Virtue
cityEvents.summary: To pay Alaric 5000 pounds of gold and 30,000 of silver, the senate stripped temple statues of their ornaments and melted some down, among them Virtus; Zosimus says courage died in Rome with it.
cityEvents.locName: temple statues of the city (unspecified)

cityEvents.title: The Basilica Aemilia burns; coins fused to the floor
cityEvents.summary: The basilica on the Forum was burned in the sack; bronze coins dropped by money-changers melted into its marble pavement, where green stains still show, and the hall was never rebuilt.
cityEvents.locName: the pavement of the Basilica Aemilia
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
cityEvents.note: Evidence archaeological (fused coins of the early 5th century); the 410 date is the accepted interpretation.

cityEvents.title: Marcella beaten by the Goths on the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: Goths burst into Marcella's house on the Aventine demanding gold; she showed her coarse tunic, was beaten, and begged only that her ward Principia be spared. They escorted both to the basilica of St Paul, where she died soon after.
cityEvents.locName: Marcella's house on the Aventine

cityEvents.title: Goths escort St Peter's treasure to the basilica
cityEvents.summary: A Goth found an elderly virgin guarding gold vessels belonging to St Peter; Alaric ordered them carried to the basilica, and Romans and Goths together sang hymns along the route under drawn swords.
cityEvents.locName: the procession to Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: The Goths enter by the Porta Salaria
cityEvents.summary: On the night of 24 August Alaric's Goths entered Rome through the Porta Salaria, opened, as later told, by treachery or by the slaves of Proba; for three days they sacked the city, the first time in 800 years an enemy had taken it.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Salaria in the Aurelian Wall

cityEvents.title: The house of Sallust set on fire
cityEvents.summary: Procopius says the Goths burned the houses next to the gate, including the house of Sallust in the gardens near the Porta Salaria, which was still standing half-burned in his own day.
cityEvents.locName: the palace in the Horti Sallustiani by the Porta Salaria

cityEvents.title: Rival popes: Eulalius holds the Lateran at Easter
cityEvents.summary: After the double election of December 418, Eulalius seized the Lateran to celebrate Easter, against the emperor's order; troops expelled him and Boniface was recognised.
cityEvents.locName: the Lateran basilica

cityEvents.title: Santa Sabina built on the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: Under Celestine I the Illyrian priest Peter built the basilica of S. Sabina, recorded in its mosaic dedication; its cypress doors carry one of the earliest crucifixion images.
cityEvents.locName: S. Sabina on the Aventine

cityEvents.title: Sixtus III builds Santa Maria Maggiore
cityEvents.summary: After the Council of Ephesus, Pope Sixtus III built the great basilica of the Mother of God on the Esquiline, its arch inscribed 'Xystus episcopus plebi Dei'.
cityEvents.locName: S. Maria Maggiore on the Esquiline

cityEvents.title: Earthquake in Rome
cityEvents.summary: An earthquake struck Rome, bringing down statues and porticoes; the Colosseum was damaged in this or later quakes.
cityEvents.locName: the city (damage to statues and porticoes)
cityEvents.note: Date and attribution uncertain; damage to the Colosseum at this time is linked by geologists to the Monte Vettore fault (Galli et al., 2019). Marker at the Colosseum as the best-attested damaged building.

cityEvents.title: Leo rebukes Romans who bow to the sun on St Peter's steps
cityEvents.summary: Preaching at Christmas, Pope Leo complained that some Christians, after climbing the steps of St Peter's, turned round and bowed to the rising sun before entering.
cityEvents.locName: the steps of Old St Peter's
cityEvents.note: Sermon datable to Leo's pontificate (440-461); year representative.

cityEvents.title: Valentinian III killed in the Campus Martius
cityEvents.summary: Watching athletes in the Campus Martius, Valentinian was struck down by Optila and Thraustila, guardsmen of the murdered Aetius, at the instigation of Petronius Maximus. The western Theodosian dynasty ended.
cityEvents.locName: the Campus Martius (some sources: 'ad duas lauros' on the Via Labicana)

cityEvents.title: Vandals strip the gilded roof of the Capitoline temple
cityEvents.summary: In fourteen days of methodical plunder the Vandals loaded their ships with the palace treasures and took half the gilded bronze roof tiles of the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus.
cityEvents.locName: the roof of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

cityEvents.title: The Jerusalem Temple treasure carried to Carthage
cityEvents.summary: Among the loot were the vessels of the Jerusalem Temple displayed by Vespasian in the Temple of Peace and kept in the palace; Belisarius brought them back from Carthage in 534.
cityEvents.locName: the Templum Pacis / palace treasury

cityEvents.title: Pope Leo meets Gaiseric at the gates
cityEvents.summary: Three days after Petronius Maximus was stoned to death fleeing the city, the Vandals arrived; Leo went out to Gaiseric and obtained that there would be no burning, killing or torture, only plunder.
cityEvents.locName: outside the gates (traditionally the Porta Portuensis, on the road from Portus)
cityEvents.note: The meeting place is not given; the Vandals came from Portus.

cityEvents.title: Sidonius prays at the apostles' tomb before entering Rome
cityEvents.summary: Arriving from Gaul in 467, Sidonius went first to the threshold of the apostles before entering the city, which he found in carnival mood for Ricimer's wedding to the emperor's daughter.
cityEvents.locName: the tomb of Peter at the Vatican

cityEvents.title: Sidonius' panegyric of Anthemius
cityEvents.summary: The Gallic aristocrat Sidonius Apollinaris delivered a verse panegyric for Anthemius' consulship before the senate and was rewarded with the prefecture of the city, from which he had to manage a grain crisis.
cityEvents.locName: the senate house

cityEvents.title: Arvandus imprisoned on the Tiber Island
cityEvents.summary: The disgraced prefect of Gaul Arvandus, convicted of treasonable letters to the Visigoths, was held on 'the island of the Epidaurian serpent' to await execution, later commuted to exile.
cityEvents.locName: the Tiber Island (former sanctuary of Aesculapius)

cityEvents.title: Ricimer's Arian church of S. Agata
cityEvents.summary: Ricimer decorated the church of the Goths on the Quirinal slope with an apse mosaic recording his gift; it served the Arian Goths until it was reconsecrated to Catholic use by Gregory the Great in 592.
cityEvents.locName: S. Agata dei Goti on the Quirinal slope

cityEvents.title: Battle at the bridge of Hadrian
cityEvents.summary: During Ricimer's siege of Anthemius, the general Bilimer came from Gaul to help the emperor and was killed fighting Ricimer's troops at the bridge by Hadrian's Mausoleum.
cityEvents.locName: the Pons Aelius before the Mausoleum of Hadrian

cityEvents.title: Anthemius beheaded in S. Crisogono
cityEvents.summary: After five months of siege and famine Ricimer's men broke in; Anthemius hid among the beggars at the church of the martyr Chrysogonus in Trastevere, where Gundobad found and beheaded him. Malalas instead places the killing at St Peter's.
cityEvents.locName: the church of S. Crisogono in Trastevere

cityEvents.title: Senators' names carved on the Colosseum seats
cityEvents.summary: Under Odoacer, the reserved seats of the amphitheatre's lower tiers were inscribed with the names of senatorial families; erased and recarved names show how the places changed hands.
cityEvents.locName: the podium seats of the Flavian Amphitheatre
cityEvents.note: Inscriptions mostly of the later 5th century; year representative.

cityEvents.title: Colosseum repaired after an earthquake
cityEvents.summary: The prefect Decius Marius Venantius Basilius restored at his own expense the arena and podium of the amphitheatre ruined by an 'abominable earthquake'.
cityEvents.locName: the arena and podium of the Flavian Amphitheatre
cityEvents.note: Earthquake of 484 or 508 (consul of 484 or 508 of the same name).

cityEvents.title: Pope Gelasius condemns the Lupercalia
cityEvents.summary: In a letter to the senator Andromachus, Gelasius attacked Christians who still kept the Lupercalia, the naked run around the Palatine, as a guarantee of fertility and health; it is the last record of the festival.
cityEvents.locName: the Lupercal and the course around the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Two popes elected on the same day
cityEvents.summary: Symmachus was consecrated in the Lateran basilica and the archpriest Laurentius, backed by the pro-Byzantine senators, in S. Maria Maggiore; Theodoric decided for Symmachus.
cityEvents.locName: the Lateran (Symmachus) and S. Maria Maggiore (Laurentius)

cityEvents.title: Theodoric received at St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: On his only visit to Rome, Theodoric went first to St Peter's 'as devoutly as a Catholic', where Pope Symmachus, the senate and the people met him with rejoicing outside the city.
cityEvents.locName: Old St Peter's on the Vatican

cityEvents.title: Theodoric speaks to the people 'at the Palm'
cityEvents.summary: Entering the city, Theodoric came to the senate and addressed the people at the place called Ad Palmam, between the Curia and the Arch of Severus, promising to keep everything the emperors had decreed.
cityEvents.locName: Ad Palmam, between the Curia and the Arch of Septimius Severus
cityEvents.note: The Palma was probably the open area by the Curia (also called Palma Aurea).

cityEvents.title: Theodoric's tricennalia: games, palace and walls
cityEvents.summary: Theodoric entered the palace in triumph, gave games in the Circus and a distribution of grain, and assigned 200 pounds of gold a year from the wine tax for repairs to the palace and the city walls.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Maximus and the Palatine palace

cityEvents.title: Count Odoin beheaded in the Sessorian palace
cityEvents.summary: The Gothic count Odoin, accused of plotting against Theodoric, was beheaded in the palace called the Sessorium by S. Croce.
cityEvents.locName: the Sessorian palace (S. Croce in Gerusalemme)

cityEvents.title: Street battles of the Laurentian schism
cityEvents.summary: For four years partisans of Laurentius held the Lateran and churches of the city while Symmachus was confined to St Peter's; clergy were killed in the streets and nuns dragged from convents.
cityEvents.locName: St Peter's (Symmachus' refuge) and the streets of Rome

cityEvents.title: Symmachus restores the Theatre of Pompey
cityEvents.summary: Theodoric asked the senator Symmachus to repair the huge, crumbling Theatre of Pompey, whose vaults, he wrote, seemed to be caves hollowed in a mountain, offering state funds.
cityEvents.locName: the Theatre of Pompey
cityEvents.note: Q. Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, father-in-law of Boethius; c. 507-511.

cityEvents.title: Theodoric orders the cloacae cleared and bronze thieves punished
cityEvents.summary: Cassiodorus' letters order the repair of the great sewers, 'so wonderful that they surpass the wonders of other cities', and the punishment of those stealing bronze and lead from monuments and aqueducts.
cityEvents.locName: the Cloaca Maxima and public monuments

cityEvents.title: Eutharic's consular games with African beasts
cityEvents.summary: For the consulship of Theodoric's son-in-law Eutharic, Rome saw beasts never seen before, sent from Africa, displayed in the amphitheatre; Cassiodorus says the people wondered at them.
cityEvents.locName: the Flavian Amphitheatre

cityEvents.title: Boethius' two sons consuls together
cityEvents.summary: Boethius watched his two young sons led as consuls from their house to the senate house by the senators and people; he gave the panegyric of Theodoric in the Curia and then distributed largesse to the crowd in the Circus. He recalled it in prison as the summit of his fortune.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia and then the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Last recorded beast hunts in the Colosseum
cityEvents.summary: Theodoric wrote to the consul Maximus approving the expense of venationes in the amphitheatre while deploring the cruelty of the beast fighters, who leapt over and dodged the animals; it is the last attested hunt.
cityEvents.locName: the arena of the Flavian Amphitheatre

cityEvents.title: Felix IV turns a Forum hall into Santi Cosma e Damiano
cityEvents.summary: With Theodoric's and Amalasuntha's gift, Pope Felix IV made the hall of the Templum Pacis behind the 'Temple of Romulus' into a church of the doctor saints, the first church in the Forum, with the apse mosaic of Christ on clouds.
cityEvents.locName: SS. Cosma e Damiano in the former hall of the Templum Pacis

cityEvents.title: Agapetus' library on the Caelian
cityEvents.summary: Pope Agapetus and Cassiodorus planned a Christian school in Rome like those of Alexandria; a library was built at Agapetus' family house on the Clivus Scauri, where an inscription 'Bibliotheca Agapeti' was found.
cityEvents.locName: the library of Agapetus on the Clivus Scauri (by S. Gregorio)

cityEvents.title: Belisarius enters by the Porta Asinaria as the Goths leave
cityEvents.summary: Invited by Pope Silverius and the people, Belisarius marched in through the Asinarian Gate on 9 December while the Gothic garrison left by the Flaminian Gate; he sent the keys of the city to Justinian.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Asinaria (Goths leaving by the Porta Flaminia)

cityEvents.title: Someone secretly tries to open the doors of Janus
cityEvents.summary: During the siege, Procopius reports, some Romans secretly tried to force open the bronze doors of the little temple of Janus in the Forum before the Curia, closed in time of peace, in the old belief that it would bring war's luck; they did not quite succeed.
cityEvents.locName: the bronze shrine of Janus in front of the Curia

cityEvents.title: Battle in the Plain of Nero
cityEvents.summary: A great sortie from the Pincian and Salarian gates and across the Tiber to the Plain of Nero routed part of the Gothic army, but the Roman citizen volunteers broke and the attack ended in retreat to the walls.
cityEvents.locName: the Campus Neronis by the Vatican

cityEvents.title: Belisarius locked out of his own city
cityEvents.summary: After fighting all day at the bridge on the Via Salaria, Belisarius rode back at nightfall to the Salarian gate covered in blood and dust; the defenders, told he was dead, would not open, and he led a last charge under the walls before being let in.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Salaria at nightfall
cityEvents.note: The battle itself was at the Pons Salarius over the Anio, just N of the model area.

cityEvents.title: Seven Gothic camps ring the city
cityEvents.summary: Witiges built six fortified camps on the left bank from the Flaminian to the Praenestine Gate and a seventh across the Tiber in the Plain of Nero by the Vatican, closing the Milvian bridge.
cityEvents.locName: the Gothic camp in the Campus Neronis by the Vatican

cityEvents.title: The Goths cut all the aqueducts
cityEvents.summary: The Goths broke all fourteen aqueducts so no water reached the city; Belisarius sealed their channels with masonry lest the enemy creep in through them. The baths of Rome fell silent and most never worked again.
cityEvents.locName: where the aqueducts enter the city at the Porta Maggiore

cityEvents.title: Belisarius' floating mills below the Janiculum
cityEvents.summary: With the Janiculum mills dry, Belisarius moored boats in the Tiber below the bridge and hung millwheels between them in the current; when the Goths sent logs and corpses downstream to wreck them, he stretched chains across the river.
cityEvents.locName: the Tiber below the bridge at the foot of the Janiculum

cityEvents.title: Belisarius shoots a Gothic chief at the Salarian gate
cityEvents.summary: As the Goths' siege towers drawn by oxen approached the Salarian gate on the day of the great assault, Belisarius laughed, shot an armoured Gothic leader through the neck, and had his archers shoot only the oxen, stranding the towers.
cityEvents.locName: the battlements of the Porta Salaria

cityEvents.title: Defenders hurl statues from Hadrian's tomb
cityEvents.summary: Attacked at close quarters at the Mausoleum of Hadrian, which formed a bastion of the wall by the Aurelian (St Peter's) gate, the defenders broke up the marble statues on its summit and threw the pieces down on the Goths.
cityEvents.locName: the summit of the Mausoleum of Hadrian
scholarship: Lanciani, The Destruction of Ancient Rome (1899)

cityEvents.title: Fight in the Vivarium by the Praenestine Gate
cityEvents.summary: At the weakest point of the wall, the Vivarium where animals for the shows had been kept, the Goths broke through the outer enclosure; Belisarius let them in and then sallied out, trapping and slaughtering them and burning their engines.
cityEvents.locName: the Vivarium between the outer and inner walls near the Porta Praenestina

cityEvents.title: The 'Broken Wall' left to St Peter's protection
cityEvents.summary: Near the Flaminian and Pincian gates a stretch of wall had long been split and leaning outward; Belisarius wished to rebuild it, but the Romans said St Peter had promised to guard it, and indeed the Goths never attacked there.
cityEvents.locName: the Muro Torto on the Pincian

cityEvents.title: Pope Silverius deposed in the Pincian palace
cityEvents.summary: Accused of corresponding with the Goths, Pope Silverius was summoned to Belisarius' headquarters in the Pincian palace, stripped of his pallium in Antonina's presence and sent into exile; Vigilius was made pope.
cityEvents.locName: the Domus Pinciana near the Porta Pinciana, Belisarius' headquarters

cityEvents.title: Goths try to enter through the Aqua Virgo channel
cityEvents.summary: During the truce the Goths crept along the dry channel of the Aqua Virgo under the Pincian, intending to come up inside the city; a guard saw a torch light and Belisarius blocked the passage.
cityEvents.locName: the channel of the Aqua Virgo under the Pincian

cityEvents.title: The Goths' fort under the aqueduct arches
cityEvents.summary: To blockade the Via Latina and Appia, the Goths walled up the arches where two aqueducts cross twice, near the later Tor Fiscale, and held it with 7000 men; the place was afterwards called the Campus Barbaricus.
cityEvents.locName: the crossing of the Aqua Claudia and Aqua Marcia arcades (Tor Fiscale)

cityEvents.title: The Goths raise the siege; carnage at the Milvian Bridge
cityEvents.summary: After a year and nine days the Goths burned their camps and withdrew across the Milvian Bridge; Belisarius attacked as they crossed and many were killed or drowned.
cityEvents.locName: the Milvian Bridge

cityEvents.title: Pope Vigilius seized at S. Cecilia
cityEvents.summary: While celebrating the feast of St Cecilia in her church in Trastevere, Vigilius was arrested by the imperial agent Anthemius and taken to a ship on the Tiber for Constantinople; the crowd threw stones after him.
cityEvents.locName: S. Cecilia in Trastevere

cityEvents.title: Famine: a father throws himself into the Tiber
cityEvents.summary: During Totila's blockade the Romans ate nettles, dogs and mice while Bessas sold grain at extortionate prices; one father of five, unable to feed his children, covered his face and leapt from a bridge into the Tiber before their eyes.
cityEvents.locName: a bridge over the Tiber
cityEvents.note: Procopius does not name the bridge.

cityEvents.title: Totila enters by the Porta Asinaria
cityEvents.summary: Four Isaurian guards let the Goths in by night through the Asinarian gate, lowering them on ropes to open it; the garrison and Bessas fled, and Totila entered a nearly empty, starving city.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Asinaria

cityEvents.title: Deacon Pelagius pleads with Totila at St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: Totila went to pray at St Peter's; the deacon Pelagius met him with the Gospels and begged him to spare the Romans, and Totila stopped the killing. Rusticiana, Boethius' widow, who had overthrown Theodoric's statues, was protected.
cityEvents.locName: Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Rome left empty of people
cityEvents.summary: Totila tore down about a third of the walls and thought of razing the city; dissuaded by Belisarius' letter, he left with the senators and removed the whole population, so that, says Procopius, no human being was left in Rome.
cityEvents.locName: the whole city

cityEvents.title: Belisarius reoccupies Rome and rebuilds the walls
cityEvents.summary: Belisarius marched into the empty city and in 25 days refilled the breaches with loose stones without mortar, planting stakes in the ditches; Totila's attacks on the half-built walls failed.
cityEvents.locName: the breached Aurelian Wall

cityEvents.title: Totila holds the last races in the Circus Maximus
cityEvents.summary: Determined to treat Rome as his own, Totila brought back senators and citizens and held horse races in the Circus Maximus, the last recorded there.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Last stand at Hadrian's tomb
cityEvents.summary: Four hundred cavalrymen under Paulus took refuge in the Mausoleum of Hadrian and the bridge before it; without food, they prepared a last charge but accepted Totila's terms, most joining his army.
cityEvents.locName: the Mausoleum of Hadrian and the Pons Aelius

cityEvents.title: Totila takes Rome by the Gate of St Paul
cityEvents.summary: Isaurian guards, unpaid for years, opened the Porta Ostiensis to the Goths at night while trumpeters made a diversion on the river side; the Byzantine garrison fled toward Centumcellae and was cut down.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Ostiensis (Porta S. Paolo)

cityEvents.title: Narses retakes Rome; keys sent to Constantinople
cityEvents.summary: After Busta Gallorum, Narses attacked Rome on several sides; Dagisthaeus scaled an undefended part of the wall, the Goths in Hadrian's tomb surrendered, and the keys of the city were sent to Justinian, the fifth capture of Rome in his reign.
cityEvents.locName: the walls and the Mausoleum of Hadrian

cityEvents.title: Pope Pelagius swears his innocence at St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: Suspected of complicity in Vigilius' death, Pelagius walked with Narses in procession from S. Pancrazio to St Peter's and, holding the Gospels and the cross over his head, swore from the ambo that he had done Vigilius no harm.
cityEvents.locName: the ambo of Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Santa Maria Antiqua in the palace vestibule
cityEvents.summary: A hall at the foot of the Palatine, once part of the imperial entrance from the Forum, was turned into the church of S. Maria Antiqua, perhaps for the Byzantine governor's court; its frescoes accumulate through the 7th and 8th centuries.
cityEvents.locName: S. Maria Antiqua at the NW foot of the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Virgil still read aloud in the Forum of Trajan
cityEvents.summary: Venantius Fortunatus, writing as he left Italy, imagines his poems being recited 'in the Forum of Trajan', where Rome still listened to Virgil being read in public.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum of Trajan

cityEvents.title: Narses rebuilds a bridge 'more admirably than before'
cityEvents.summary: After the Gothic wars Narses restored bridges around Rome destroyed by Totila; the inscription of the Pons Salarius records his victory over the Goths.
cityEvents.locName: the Via Salaria out of the Porta Salaria (bridge just beyond the model area)

cityEvents.title: Pelagius II rebuilds S. Lorenzo during the Lombard siege
cityEvents.summary: During the Lombard siege of Rome Pope Pelagius II rebuilt the shrine of St Lawrence on the Via Tiburtina, cutting it into the hillside; he appears in the arch mosaic offering the church.
cityEvents.locName: S. Lorenzo fuori le mura

cityEvents.title: Great Tiber flood: serpents and a dragon swept to the sea
cityEvents.summary: In November 589 the Tiber overflowed the walls and flooded much of the city, ruining churches and the papal granaries; Gregory of Tours' deacon saw a multitude of snakes and a great dragon carried down to the sea. Plague followed.
cityEvents.locName: the low city and the walls along the Tiber

cityEvents.title: Sevenfold litany: the clergy set out from SS. Cosma e Damiano
cityEvents.summary: Gregory ordered a sevenfold procession for three days; the clergy were to set out from the church of SS. Cosma e Damiano in the Forum, chanting, toward S. Maria Maggiore.
cityEvents.locName: SS. Cosma e Damiano in the Forum

cityEvents.title: Litany: the abbots set out from SS. Gervasio e Protasio
cityEvents.summary: The abbots and their monks gathered at the church of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, the titulus of Vestina (S. Vitale), at the foot of the Quirinal.
cityEvents.locName: SS. Gervasio e Protasio (S. Vitale) in the valley below the Quirinal

cityEvents.title: Litany: the abbesses set out from SS. Marcellino e Pietro
cityEvents.summary: The abbesses with their nuns set out from the church of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter near the Lateran.
cityEvents.locName: SS. Marcellino e Pietro on the Via Labicana by the Lateran

cityEvents.title: Litany: the children set out from SS. Giovanni e Paolo
cityEvents.summary: The children of Rome were assembled at the church of John and Paul on the Caelian.
cityEvents.locName: SS. Giovanni e Paolo on the Clivus Scauri, Caelian

cityEvents.title: Litany: the laymen set out from S. Stefano
cityEvents.summary: The laymen gathered at the church of the protomartyr Stephen, usually identified with S. Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian.
cityEvents.locName: S. Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian

cityEvents.title: Litany: the widows set out from S. Eufemia
cityEvents.summary: The widows gathered at the church of St Euphemia on the Vicus Patricius below the Esquiline.
cityEvents.locName: S. Eufemia on the Vicus Patricius (destroyed)

cityEvents.title: Litany: the married women set out from S. Clemente
cityEvents.summary: The married women gathered at the church of St Clement in the valley between the Caelian and the Esquiline.
cityEvents.locName: S. Clemente

cityEvents.title: Eighty fall dead during the litany
cityEvents.summary: As the seven processions converged on S. Maria Maggiore, chanting Kyrie eleison, eighty people collapsed and died within an hour, yet Gregory continued preaching and the procession went on.
cityEvents.locName: the converging processions at S. Maria Maggiore

cityEvents.title: The angel sheathing his sword over Hadrian's tomb
cityEvents.summary: Later legend says that as Gregory's procession crossed toward St Peter's, he saw the archangel Michael on top of Hadrian's Mausoleum sheathing a bloody sword, a sign that the plague had ended; the monument has been Castel Sant'Angelo since.
cityEvents.locName: the summit of the Mausoleum of Hadrian
cityEvents.note: The vision is first recorded in the 13th century; contemporary sources do not mention it.

cityEvents.title: Pope Pelagius II dies of the plague
cityEvents.summary: The plague that followed the flood struck the clergy first; Pelagius II died among the first victims in February 590 and the deacon Gregory was chosen to succeed him.
cityEvents.locName: buried at St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Gregory consecrated bishop at St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: After trying to flee, Gregory was consecrated pope at St Peter's on 3 September 590, once the emperor Maurice's confirmation arrived.
cityEvents.locName: Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Gregory sees Romans led off roped by the neck
cityEvents.summary: With the Lombard king Agilulf before the walls, Gregory broke off his sermons on Ezekiel: from the walls he had seen Romans led away with ropes round their necks like dogs to be sold in Gaul.
cityEvents.locName: the Aurelian Wall (Agilulf's army before the city)

cityEvents.title: Augustine's mission leaves St Andrew's on the Caelian
cityEvents.summary: Gregory sent Augustine, prior of his own monastery of St Andrew on the Clivus Scauri, his family's house, with about forty monks to convert the English.
cityEvents.locName: the monastery of St Andrew on the Clivus Scauri (S. Gregorio al Celio)

cityEvents.title: Images of Phocas and Leontia acclaimed at the Lateran
cityEvents.summary: The portraits of the new emperor Phocas and his wife arrived in Rome and were acclaimed by clergy and senate in the Lateran basilica: 'Hear us, Christ! Long life to Phocas Augustus!'; Gregory had them placed in the oratory of St Caesarius in the Palatine palace.
cityEvents.locName: the Lateran basilica, then the oratory of St Caesarius on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Gregory the Great buried in the portico of St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: Gregory died after years of illness and was buried in the portico of St Peter's, where his epitaph called him 'God's consul'. A famine followed and the people turned against his memory.
cityEvents.locName: the portico of Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Column of Phocas: the last monument of the Forum
cityEvents.summary: The exarch Smaragdus set a gilded statue of the emperor Phocas on a reused fluted column in front of the Rostra, 'for the innumerable benefits of his piety and the peace procured for Italy'; Phocas was overthrown two years later.
cityEvents.locName: in front of the Rostra in the Forum

cityEvents.title: The Pantheon becomes S. Maria ad Martyres
cityEvents.summary: With Phocas' permission Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as a church of the Virgin and all martyrs, bringing in bones from the catacombs; it became the first pagan temple in Rome turned into a church, which saved it.
cityEvents.locName: the Pantheon (S. Maria ad Martyres)
cityEvents.note: The traditional date of 13 May 609 (possibly 610 or 613).

cityEvents.title: Earthquake followed by a skin plague
cityEvents.summary: Under Pope Deusdedit a great earthquake struck in August, followed by an epidemic of 'scabies' so disfiguring that the dead could not be recognised.
cityEvents.locName: the city

cityEvents.title: Pope Deusdedit dies after the earthquake and plague
cityEvents.summary: Deusdedit, who had personally cared for the sick in the epidemic after the earthquake, died and was buried in St Peter's, leaving a bequest of a full year's stipend to all his clergy.
cityEvents.locName: burial at Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Bronze roof tiles of the Temple of Roma taken for St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: With the emperor Heraclius' consent, Pope Honorius I stripped the gilded bronze tiles from 'the temple called of Rome', the Temple of Venus and Roma, to roof St Peter's.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Venus and Roma

cityEvents.title: The senate house becomes the church of Sant'Adriano
cityEvents.summary: Honorius I turned the Curia Iulia, the senate house rebuilt by Diocletian, into the church of S. Adriano 'in Tribus Fatis', which preserved its walls and bronze doors.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia Iulia (S. Adriano)

cityEvents.title: Honorius rebuilds Sant'Agnese over the martyr's tomb
cityEvents.summary: Honorius built a new galleried basilica on the Via Nomentana sunk to the level of St Agnes' tomb in the catacomb, with the apse mosaic showing the saint between two popes.
cityEvents.locName: S. Agnese fuori le mura on the Via Nomentana

cityEvents.title: Honorius I rebuilds S. Pancrazio on the Janiculum
cityEvents.summary: Honorius I rebuilt the basilica over the tomb of the boy martyr Pancras on the Via Aurelia outside the Porta Aurelia, where oaths were sworn on the saint's relics.
cityEvents.locName: S. Pancrazio on the Via Aurelia

cityEvents.title: Bronze of the Curia doors and Rostra survive the conversion
cityEvents.summary: When the Curia became the church of S. Adriano, its Diocletianic bronze doors were left in place; they were moved to the Lateran in the 17th century, where they still hang.
cityEvents.locName: the bronze doors of the Curia Iulia

cityEvents.title: The Lateran treasury plundered by the imperial army
cityEvents.summary: With the see vacant, the chartularius Maurice incited the unpaid army to besiege the Lateran for three days, then sealed its treasure, and the exarch Isaac came from Ravenna to seize it and send part to Heraclius.
cityEvents.locName: the Lateran episcopium and treasury
cityEvents.note: Event of 640, before Severinus' consecration (28 May 640).

cityEvents.title: John IV builds the chapel of S. Venanzio
cityEvents.summary: The Dalmatian pope John IV built an oratory beside the Lateran baptistery for relics of martyrs brought from Dalmatia and Istria, ravaged by the Avars and Slavs; its mosaic survives.
cityEvents.locName: the oratory of S. Venanzio by the Lateran baptistery
